about: Proven drink structures the generator builds from (see web/lib/composer.js). Compiled from research by scripts/archetypes-build.mjs.

archetypes.name: Planter's Punch & Caribbean Rum Punch
archetypes.definition: A single-serve Caribbean rum punch built on the 'one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak' rhyme: dark or aged rum with lime, sugar, generous dilution and a finish of Angostura and grated nutmeg.
classics: Planter's Punch (Jamaican / Myrtle Bank Hotel style)

signature.note: Jamaican is the default; Bajan for a Barbados rum punch. At least half the base must be a dark/aged rum unless it is the Jamaican overproof party punch.
Lime first; lemon only as a partner (Vic used both).
Sugar or cane syrup; grenadine (Jamaican strawberry syrup) gives the red version.
The fifth element of punch. Angostura dashes and/or grated nutmeg on top; 'a touch of spice to make it nice'.

optional.note: The 'four of weak'. Ice melt counts; island punches use juice; Vic topped with soda.
Floridita added curaçao; Smuggler's Cove adds allspice dram.
A funk or proof booster alongside the main rum.

canonicalSpecs.name: Planter's Punch (1908 rhyme)
canonicalSpecs.source: Verse in The New York Times, 8 Aug 1908: 'two of sour, one and a half of sweet, three of strong, four of weak' (Old Jamaica rum)
canonicalSpecs.note: The verse names no spice; nutmeg was the custom. The 'four of weak' meant water AND ice, so shaking 2 oz water over crushed ice double-counts dilution - use 1 oz water or build it.

canonicalSpecs.name: Bajan Rum Punch (1-2-3-4)
canonicalSpecs.source: Barbadian folk formula 'one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak' (same ratio in Baker, Gentleman's Companion II, 1939)
canonicalSpecs.note: Taken literally the rhyme is sweet (s:a ~20); Bajan bars usually cut the syrup or let fruit juice be part of the sweet.

canonicalSpecs.name: Planter's Punch, Angostura Bar (Trinidad, 1934)
canonicalSpecs.source: Angostura Recipes - 42 Cocktails (Angostura-Wuppermann, 1934)
canonicalSpecs.note: Liqueur-glass parts; a full teaspoon of Angostura is the Trinidadian signature.

canonicalSpecs.name: Trader Vic's Planter's Punch (1946)
canonicalSpecs.source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946), p. 61
canonicalSpecs.note: Red Heart or Myers's; very tart by modern taste.

canonicalSpecs.name: Planter's Punch (Smuggler's Cove)
canonicalSpecs.source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)

canonicalSpecs.name: Jamaican Rum Punch (island party style)
canonicalSpecs.source: Jamaican home tradition, cf. Appleton/Wray & Nephew 'K11' punch and Grace strawberry-syrup recipes

lines.note: stands in for Jamaican strawberry syrup

ratios.notes: Drier and stronger in the Smuggler's Cove line (s:a ~9), sweeter and longer in island punches (s:a ~14). The rhyme is a starting point; nobody actually uses two full parts of 2:1 syrup.

required: grated nutmeg or an Angostura top

archetypes.look: Tall glass of crushed ice; body translucent amber-to-garnet (molasses rum plus grenadine reads ruby-amber; the plain sugar version is clear honey-amber; the Jamaican party punch is an opaque coral-red from juice and red syrup). A brownish speckle of nutmeg on the ice cap, sometimes a dark Angostura blush on top. No foam, no layers beyond the bitters.
substitutions: Bajan aged rum for the Jamaican (it becomes a Barbados rum punch)
demerara syrup for white sugar
grenadine for half the sugar (red Jamaican style)
soda water for still water (Vic)
a barspoon of allspice dram for the bitters
Smith & Cross for part of the aged Jamaican to add funk
redFlags: No spice at all: no bitters, no nutmeg, no allspice (it is just a rum sour)
Light white column rum as the only rum: punch needs molasses weight
Pineapple + orange + grenadine so heavy it becomes a resort fruit punch with no lime edge
Calling it 'Planter's Punch' and serving it up in a coupe
Served without dilution - the weak is part of the formula
prayerFit: groups and parties (scales to a bowl)

archetypes.name: Fish House Punch & Bowl Punches
archetypes.definition: An 18th-century communal punch: lemon and sugar (ideally an oleo-saccharum), a split base of brandy and rum (with peach brandy or Batavia arrack), lengthened with cold water or tea and served from a bowl over a block of ice with nutmeg on top.

signature.note: Jamaican rum is the traditional rum; arrack for the oldest punches.
Cognac plus peach brandy (dry, aged) in a Fish House Punch. The vocabulary only has sweet peach liqueur - cut the sugar if you use it.
Lemon is traditional in Anglo-American punch.
Ideally sugar muddled with lemon peels until oily.
Cold water or black tea; a splash of sparkling wine in arrack punches.

canonicalSpecs.name: Fish House Punch (Jerry Thomas, 1862) per cup
canonicalSpecs.source: Jerry Thomas, How to Mix Drinks (1862), No. 46 - bowl recipe scaled to 1/12
canonicalSpecs.note: Historically very sweet and gentle; bowl: 1/3 pint lemon, 3/4 lb sugar, 1/2 pint Cognac, 1/4 pint peach brandy, 1/4 pint Jamaica rum, 2 1/2 pints water.

canonicalSpecs.name: Fish House Punch (single serve)
canonicalSpecs.source: Difford's Guide, 'Fish House Punch' (with cold black tea)

canonicalSpecs.name: Arrack Punch (Boothby, 1908)
canonicalSpecs.source: William Boothby, The World's Drinks and How to Mix Them (1908), No. 327
canonicalSpecs.note: Boothby's "large spoonful" of sugar is interpreted.

ratios.notes: Bowl punches are sweeter and weaker than cocktails - built to be drunk by the cup for hours. Scale x10-20 for a bowl; use a single big block of ice.

typical: a single block of ice in the bowl

archetypes.look: Clear-to-hazy pale gold amber, glinting in a wide punch bowl around a single block of ice, lemon wheels and a freckling of nutmeg on the surface; ladled into small cups. No foam, no layers.
substitutions: cold black tea for half the water
Smith & Cross for the Jamaica rum (cut quantity)
applejack for the peach brandy (an American cider-orchard punch)
Batavia arrack for half the rum
demerara sugar in the oleo-saccharum
redFlags: Served as a single short shaken sour in a coupe and still called a bowl punch
Lime + grenadine + pineapple: that is a resort punch, not a Philadelphia punch
Peach schnapps as the only peach with no brandy
Too strong to drink by the cup

archetypes.name: Ti' Punch
archetypes.definition: The French Caribbean petit punch: two ounces of rhum agricole, a coin of lime with its peel squeezed and dropped in, and a barspoon of cane syrup, stirred briefly in a small glass with little or no ice; each drinker builds their own.

signature.note: Blanc (often 50-55%) is the everyday serve; vieux for an after-dinner one.
A disc cut from the side of the lime with skin, pinched over the glass: oil and a few drops of juice, not a measured sour.
Sirop de canne; rich-simple is the vocabulary stand-in.

canonicalSpecs.name: Ti' Punch (Smuggler's Cove)
canonicalSpecs.source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)

lines.note: one coin of lime, squeezed and dropped in

canonicalSpecs.name: Ti' Punch (Martinique, traditional)
canonicalSpecs.source: Martinique practice as described by PUNCH and Rhum J.M. (half barspoon sirop, a small lime coin, 100-proof blanc)

canonicalSpecs.name: Ti' Punch Vieux
canonicalSpecs.source: Smuggler's Cove (2016)

ratios.notes: Essentially neat rum seasoned with lime oil and cane sugar. No dilution beyond a single cube. Do not let the balance engine "fix" it into a daiquiri.

required: the lime coin itself, in the glass
typical: a small bois lélé swizzle stick

archetypes.look: A short, mostly empty rocks glass holding two fingers of water-clear (blanc) or pale gold (vieux) rhum with a single green lime coin and maybe one cube. Faint oil sheen; no haze, no foam.
substitutions: Haitian clairin or cane rum for agricole (it becomes a cousin, not a Ti' Punch)
agricole vieux for blanc
a teaspoon of rich demerara syrup for cane syrup
one ice cube for none
redFlags: A full ounce of lime juice (that is a daiquiri)
Crushed ice, fruit juice or soda
Big tiki garnish - it is a rum-shop drink

archetypes.name: Grog (naval)
archetypes.definition: Navy rum cut with water, sharpened with lime and softened with sugar - the 1740 Royal Navy ration that became a plain, bracing rum sour-highball.

signature.note: British navy-style rum (Demerara-led) is the soul of it.
Lime juice was the anti-scurvy ration.
Brown sugar or honey.

optional.note: The defining dilution of the original (4:1 water to rum in 1740).

canonicalSpecs.name: Grog (single serve)
canonicalSpecs.source: Difford's Guide, 'Grog' (after Vernon's 1740 order)

canonicalSpecs.name: Grog (Smuggler's Cove)
canonicalSpecs.source: Smuggler's Cove (2016), via SBoudrias/cocktails transcription

canonicalSpecs.name: Vernon's ration (1740, illustrative)
canonicalSpecs.source: Admiral Edward Vernon's order of 21 Aug 1740 (one quart water to each half pint rum; lime and sugar bought by the men)
canonicalSpecs.note: Historical curiosity; served warm from the scuttlebutt. Do not generate this literally.

ratios.notes: A simple drink; its character comes from the rum. Dilution water is welcome.

archetypes.look: Plain, rustic: translucent clear amber-brown over cubes in a tumbler, a lime wedge. No foam, no layers.
substitutions: honey for sugar (Honey Rum Grog)
Demerara rum for navy blend
a dash of Angostura for nothing

archetypes.name: Navy Grog
archetypes.definition: Three ounces of three different rums with equal lime and white grapefruit, sweetened with honey (Don) or demerara and allspice dram (Vic), served over an ice cone with a straw through it.

signature.note: Light + dark Jamaican + Demerara is the classic triad.
White, not pink.
Don: 1 oz honey mix. Vic: 1/4 oz demerara + 1/4 oz allspice dram.

canonicalSpecs.name: Navy Grog (Don the Beachcomber)
canonicalSpecs.source: Don the Beachcomber, c. 1941; Jeff Berry (Grog Log 1998; Beachbum Berry Remixed 2010); Wikipedia

lines.orig: white Cuban / light Puerto Rican rum

garnish: ice cone with a straw through it
canonicalSpecs.note: Shake with ice and pour into a double old fashioned around a shaved-ice cone (packed in a pilsner, bored with a chopstick for the straw, frozen overnight).

canonicalSpecs.name: Navy Grog (Trader Vic's)
canonicalSpecs.source: Trader Vic's, 1940s; per Smuggler's Cove / Wikipedia

canonicalSpecs.name: Navy Grog (Tropical Standard)
canonicalSpecs.source: Garret Richard & Ben Schaffer, Tropical Standard (2023)

ratios.notes: Equal lime and white grapefruit; Don's honey version is the rounder (10:1), Vic's demerara + allspice version the drier (5.5:1).

required: straw through an ice cone (or crushed ice)

archetypes.look: A tall white cylinder of frozen shaved ice (the cone) standing in a double old fashioned with a straw down its center; around it a cloudy amber-tan liquid (honey + grapefruit + dark rums), a few fine bubbles from the soda. No layers.
substitutions: Hamilton 86 or El Dorado 5/8 for Demerara
Coruba or Hamilton Pot Still Black for dark Jamaican
Barbancourt white or Flor de Caña 4 for light rum
crushed ice if no cone
redFlags: navy-strength Pusser's alone called a Navy Grog

archetypes.name: Queen's Park Swizzle & Trinidad Swizzles
archetypes.definition: A Demerara-rum swizzle in the Trinidad style: mint pressed in the bottom, lime and sugar, crushed ice churned with a bois lélé until the glass frosts, and a heavy crown of Angostura bitters on top.

signature.note: Demerara (Guyana) is canonical; Trinidad column rum also fits.
6-10 leaves pressed gently in the bottom, never shredded.
4-8 dashes on top of the ice cap.

optional.note: Modern bars layer Peychaud's for a red band.

canonicalSpecs.name: Queen's Park Swizzle (Trader Vic, 1946)
canonicalSpecs.source: Trader Vic's Book of Food and Drink (1946) / Bartender's Guide (1947): 'the most delightful form of anesthesia given out today'

lines.note: juice of 1/2 large lime, shell dropped in

canonicalSpecs.note: Vic swizzles the bitters in; the layered crown is a modern presentation.

canonicalSpecs.name: Queen's Park Swizzle (modern, PUNCH)
canonicalSpecs.source: PUNCH, 'Queen's Park Swizzle' (modern standard)

canonicalSpecs.name: Queen's Park Swizzle (Smuggler's Cove)
canonicalSpecs.source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)

canonicalSpecs.name: West Indian Swizzle (Angostura, 1924)
canonicalSpecs.source: Angostura Bitters Centenary Gift Book (Trinidad, 1924)
canonicalSpecs.note: Early swizzles were bitters-and-sugar drinks with no citrus; shows the bitters lineage.

ratios.notes: A short-ingredient, high-rum drink; the ice does the lengthening. Bitters crown counts as flavour, not volume.

required: Angostura bitters crown on the ice
typical: bois lélé swizzle stick left in

archetypes.look: The famous tri-colour: a band of bright green bruised mint leaves at the bottom, a pale gold-amber rum-and-lime middle in frosted crushed ice, and a rust-red Angostura crown bleeding down from the top. The outside of the glass is white with frost.
substitutions: demerara syrup for white sugar
El Dorado 8/12 or Hamilton 86 for any Demerara
falernum for half the sugar
Peychaud's under the Angostura for a two-tone crown
redFlags: Light rum (then it is a Mojito without soda)
Served in a coupe or with cubed ice

archetypes.name: Bermuda Rum Swizzle
archetypes.definition: Bermuda's national drink: Gosling's Black and Gold Seal rums with orange and pineapple juices, lemon, falernum and Angostura, swizzled by the pitcher until frothy.
classics: Rum Swizzle (Swizzle Inn, Bailey's Bay, Bermuda, 1932)

signature.note: Black Seal plus a gold rum (Gosling's Gold; the 1930s used a Barbados rum).
Lemon in the Swizzle Inn spec; Difford adds lime and pink grapefruit.
Both orange and pineapple.

canonicalSpecs.name: Rum Swizzle (Swizzle Inn)
canonicalSpecs.source: Swizzle Inn, Bailey's Bay, Bermuda - pitcher for six, scaled to one (via Wikipedia 'Rum swizzle' / Go To Bermuda)

canonicalSpecs.name: Bermuda Rum Swizzle (Difford's)
canonicalSpecs.source: Difford's Guide, 'Bermuda Rum Swizzle' (adapted from Swizzle Inn via Del Pedro)

ratios.notes: Juicy and gentle, a party drink by the jug. The froth comes from swizzling pineapple juice hard.

archetypes.look: Opaque sunset orange-amber with a pale frothy head (from swizzling the pineapple), poured from a pitcher over ice in a tall glass; orange slice and cherry. No distinct layers.
substitutions: Bajan gold rum for Gosling's Gold
falernum syrup for liqueur (cut triple sec)
shaken until frothy and strained into a stemmed glass (the Inn's old method)
redFlags: Mint and Angostura crown (that is the Queen's Park)

archetypes.name: 151 Swizzle
archetypes.definition: A small, ferocious swizzle of 151-proof Demerara rum with lime, sugar, a dash of Angostura and a few drops of Pernod, flash-blended with crushed ice and served in a frosted flared metal cup dusted with nutmeg.

signature.note: Lemon Hart / Hamilton 151 Demerara.
6 drops Pernod or Herbsaint.

canonicalSpecs.name: 151 Swizzle (Don the Beachcomber)
canonicalSpecs.source: Jeff Berry, Sippin' Safari (2007) / Beachbum Berry Remixed; beachbumberry.com

canonicalSpecs.name: 151 Swizzle (Mai-Kai reconstruction)
canonicalSpecs.source: The Atomic Grog (Hurricane Hayward) tribute recipe
canonicalSpecs.note: Reconstruction; sweeter than Don's.

ratios.notes: Tiny but strong; dilution from crushed ice is essential. Never more than 1.5 oz of 151 per serve.

never: fire (it is not a flaming drink)

archetypes.look: A flared metal cup sweating thick white frost; inside, a mound of crushed ice tinted pale caramel by the rum, dusted brown with nutmeg, a cinnamon stick standing up. Little liquid visible.
substitutions: Hamilton 151 for Lemon Hart 151
Herbsaint for Pernod
falernum for half the sugar (Mai-Kai)
a julep cup for the swizzle cup
redFlags: Served in a tall glass with lots of mixer

archetypes.name: Chartreuse & Green Swizzle
archetypes.definition: A swizzle whose base is herbal - green Chartreuse, or rum/gin dosed with wormwood - balanced with lime and falernum (plus pineapple in the Chartreuse version) and finished with nutmeg or Angostura.

signature.note: Chartreuse as base (1.25 oz) or absinthe as a barspoon accent on rum/gin.

canonicalSpecs.name: Chartreuse Swizzle (Dionysos, 2003)
canonicalSpecs.source: Marcovaldo Dionysos; PUNCH, Imbibe, Smuggler's Cove (2016)

canonicalSpecs.name: Green Swizzle (Wondrich)
canonicalSpecs.source: David Wondrich, via Tasting Table; cf. Oxford Companion to Spirits & Cocktails

ratios.notes: Chartreuse brings its own sugar and 55% ABV, so it acts as base + sweetener. baseOz here counts only true base spirits.

archetypes.look: Chartreuse Swizzle: opaque, luminous pale chartreuse-green/yellow in frosted crushed ice, nutmeg freckles and a mint sprig on top. Green Swizzle: pale cloudy greenish-white body (absinthe louche) with a rust Angostura crown.
substitutions: yellow Chartreuse for half the green (softer)
absinthe rinse for absinthe barspoon
gin for rum in the Green Swizzle
redFlags: Crème de menthe used to fake the green

archetypes.name: Dark 'n Stormy
archetypes.definition: Bermuda's highball of spicy ginger beer over ice with black rum floated on top so it hangs like a storm cloud, a lime wedge on the side.
classics: Dark 'n Stormy (bartender's version with lime juice)

signature.note: Gosling's Black Seal is the trademarked original.
Spicy ginger beer, not ginger ale.

optional.note: Wedge squeezed, or a measured splash in bartender versions.

canonicalSpecs.name: Dark 'n Stormy (Gosling's official)
canonicalSpecs.source: Gosling's Rum trademark recipe: 1.5 oz Black Seal, 4-5 oz ginger beer, lime wedge

canonicalSpecs.name: Dark 'n Stormy (IBA)
canonicalSpecs.source: IBA official list (New Era Drinks)

canonicalSpecs.name: Dark 'n Stormy (with lime and bitters)
canonicalSpecs.source: Difford's Guide adaptation

ratios.notes: Sweetness comes from ginger beer; acid is optional. Ratio ~1 rum : 2.5-3 ginger beer.

archetypes.look: Two-tone highball over clear cubes: the lower body hazy pale straw-gold ginger beer with fine bubbles; the top quarter a dark mahogany-black rum cloud bleeding down in tendrils ('the storm'). Lime wedge on the rim.
substitutions: any black blended rum (but only Gosling's may legally carry the name)
a squeeze of lime juice
Angostura dashes
redFlags: Ginger ale instead of ginger beer
White or gold rum (that is a Mule/Buck)
Rum stirred in so there is no storm cloud

archetypes.name: Rum & Gin Mules (Jamaican Mule, Gin-Gin Mule)
archetypes.definition: A spirit-lime-ginger highball in the Moscow Mule mould - spirit, fresh lime and sharp ginger beer (or ginger syrup plus soda) over ice, often with mint - served in a copper mug or highball.

signature.note: Jamaican rum for the Jamaican Mule; London dry gin for the Gin-Gin.
Ginger beer top, or ginger syrup shaken in.

optional.note: Gin-Gin uses 1 oz simple with only 1 oz homemade ginger beer.

canonicalSpecs.name: Gin-Gin Mule (Pegu Club)
canonicalSpecs.source: Audrey Saunders (Beacon, 2000; Pegu Club); James Beard Foundation archive

canonicalSpecs.name: Jamaican Mule (Easy Tiki)
canonicalSpecs.source: Punch, Easy Tiki (2021), Jelani Johnson

canonicalSpecs.name: Jamaican Mule (copper-mug highball)
canonicalSpecs.source: Common modern build (Moscow Mule template with Jamaican rum)

ratios.notes: Ginger heat should be noticeable; lime keeps it crisp.

archetypes.look: Pale, hazy straw-gold (gin) to light amber (Jamaican rum) in a sweating copper mug or highball with fine bubbles; flecks of mint green in the Gin-Gin; mint sprig and lime wheel on top.
substitutions: ginger syrup + soda for ginger beer
gin for rum (Gin-Gin)
Smith & Cross for half the Jamaican rum
pineapple splash for tiki lean

archetypes.name: Suffering Bastard & its brothers
archetypes.definition: Joe Scialom's wartime hangover cure: equal gin and brandy (or bourbon) with lime, Angostura and ginger beer, served long with mint and orange.
classics: Suffering Bastard (Joe Scialom, Shepheard's Hotel Cairo, 1942)

signature.note: Gin + brandy (Suffering); + bourbon (Dying); + rum (Dead).
Rose's lime cordial in Scialom's notes per Berry; fresh lime + a little sugar today.
2 dashes.

canonicalSpecs.name: Suffering Bastard (Scialom, 1942)
canonicalSpecs.source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), from Scialom's papers

canonicalSpecs.name: Suffering Bastard (Smuggler's Cove)
canonicalSpecs.source: Smuggler's Cove (2016)

canonicalSpecs.name: Dead Bastard
canonicalSpecs.source: Berry, Remixed (2010) - Scialom's four-spirit escalation

ratios.notes: Shake the spirits, lime and bitters; top with ginger beer (or shake briefly with it).

archetypes.look: Tall, hazy pale gold-amber, lightly effervescent over cubes; a mint sprig and orange half-wheel. No layers.
substitutions: bourbon for brandy (Dying Bastard)
fresh lime + 1/4 oz demerara for cordial
redFlags: Confusing it with Trader Vic's unrelated rum-orgeat Suffering Bastard

archetypes.name: Daiquiri
archetypes.definition: Rum, fresh lime and sugar, shaken hard with ice and strained into a chilled coupe - the purest rum sour, with nothing to hide behind.

signature.note: Light Cuban-style is classic; any good rum makes a daiquiri, but name it accordingly.
Lime only - lemon makes it a Rum Sour.
Plain sugar/syrup.

optional.note: A barspoon of an accent at most; more and it becomes a named variant.

canonicalSpecs.name: Daiquiri No. 1 (El Floridita)
canonicalSpecs.source: Cocktails Bar La Florida (Havana, 1934; 1939 eds.)
canonicalSpecs.note: Floridita shook with shaved ice and strained; Cuban sugar measures were generous.

canonicalSpecs.name: Daiquiri (IBA)
canonicalSpecs.source: IBA official list (The Unforgettables)

canonicalSpecs.name: Daiquiri No. 1 (Smuggler's Cove)
canonicalSpecs.source: Smuggler's Cove (2016)

canonicalSpecs.name: Daiquiri (modern craft standard)
canonicalSpecs.source: Widely taught 2 : 1 : 3/4 build (e.g. Death & Co, 2014)

ratios.notes: Modern balance ~ 8:1 sugar:acid by weight. Historical Cuban specs read tarter on paper (s:a ~5) because a Cuban teaspoon of superfine sugar was heaped; generate at 7.5-9.

archetypes.look: Served up in a chilled coupe, no ice: a pale, slightly cloudy white-gold liquid with the faintest green cast and a thin layer of fine white froth/ice shards on top. Glass beaded with condensation.
substitutions: lightly aged Jamaican for light rum (name it a Jamaican Daiquiri)
demerara syrup for simple
a few drops of saline
agricole blanc for a grassier daiquiri
redFlags: Blended with strawberry syrup and still called a classic Daiquiri
On the rocks in a highball

archetypes.name: Hemingway Daiquiri (Papa Doble)
archetypes.definition: Constante's daiquiri for Hemingway: white rum, lime, grapefruit and maraschino with little or no added sugar, shaken or blended with shaved ice.

signature.note: White grapefruit originally.
Luxardo-style, cherry-pit and floral.

canonicalSpecs.name: E. Hemingway Special (Floridita, 1939)
canonicalSpecs.source: Bar La Florida, Cuña del Daiquirí (1939)

canonicalSpecs.name: Papa Doble
canonicalSpecs.source: A. E. Hotchner, Papa Hemingway (1966): 2 1/2 jiggers Bacardi, juice of two limes and half a grapefruit, six drops maraschino, frozen
canonicalSpecs.note: A double, bone-dry, frozen. A curiosity for the strong-willed.

canonicalSpecs.name: Hemingway Special (IBA)
canonicalSpecs.source: IBA official list (Contemporary Classics)

ratios.notes: Deliberately dry and bitter-edged; maraschino and grapefruit are the only sweetness in the purist versions.

archetypes.look: Up in a coupe: pale, cloudy whitish-yellow (white grapefruit) or faint blush-pink (pink grapefruit), fine froth; frozen version is a snowy white-yellow slush mounded in a goblet.
substitutions: pink grapefruit for white (sweeter, blush colour)
1/4 oz simple for modern palates
frozen with shaved ice (Papa Doble)
redFlags: Missing maraschino or grapefruit (then it is just a daiquiri)

archetypes.name: Frozen Daiquiri (Frappé)
archetypes.definition: A daiquiri (rum, lime, sugar and at most one fruit or liqueur) blended with finely crushed ice into a fine, spoonable snow, the frappé Constantino Ribalaigua perfected at El Floridita. It is built bolder than a shaken daiquiri because the cold and the ice mute both sugar and acid.

signature.note: White Cuban-style rum is canonical.
Frozen drinks need more sugar than shaken ones because cold dulls sweetness.

optional.note: One fruit at most; frozen or ripe fruit doubles as ice.
The Floridita No. 3 uses 1 tsp of grapefruit juice.

canonicalSpecs.name: Daiquiri No. 4 (Florida Style)
canonicalSpecs.source: Bar La Florida (El Floridita), Havana, 1930s house booklet; Constantino Ribalaigua Vert
canonicalSpecs.note: Electric mixer with shaved ice; served frappé.

canonicalSpecs.name: Daiquiri No. 3
canonicalSpecs.source: Bar La Florida, Havana, 1930s; Punch / Oxford Companion
canonicalSpecs.note: Served frappé.

canonicalSpecs.name: Strawberry Daiquiri (frozen)
canonicalSpecs.source: Common published spec (Liquor.com, Difford's), recalled

canonicalSpecs.name: Banana Daiquiri (frozen)
canonicalSpecs.source: Caribbean resort composite (claimed by Mountain Top, St. Thomas, among others); recalled, not verified

ratios.notes: The Floridita frappés are deliberately dry (ratio about 5). Modern fruit frozen daiquiris run 7.5-10.5 because the fruit adds sugar and the cold mutes it. Use about 1 cup (6 oz) of ice per 4 oz of liquid; less when fruit is frozen.

archetypes.look: Opaque, frosty and matte, with fine snow-like crystals, domed above the rim. Air and ice pale whatever fruit is in it: strawberry turns coral-pink, banana pale cream, and the plain lime daiquiri is frosted white with a faint green-yellow cast. One color throughout.
substitutions: agricole blanc for Cuban-style rum
one fruit for another
a frozen fruit as part of the ice
redFlags: Cream or coconut (then it is a colada or a coconut daiquiri)
Under-sweetened, which tastes sour and thin once frozen

archetypes.name: Fruit Daiquiri (Banana, Pineapple, Passion Fruit)
archetypes.definition: A daiquiri in which a named fruit - real fruit, juice, purée or a fruit liqueur backed by fruit - joins rum, lime and sugar, shaken up or blended frozen.
classics: Banana Daiquiri (Mountain Top, St. Thomas lore)

signature.note: Aged or Jamaican rum loves banana; light rum for pineapple and passion fruit.
Lime by default.
The fruit in the name must be present at a tasteable dose; banana liqueur alone is acceptable shaken, real banana required frozen.

canonicalSpecs.name: Frozen Banana Daiquiri (Tropical Standard)
canonicalSpecs.source: Tropical Standard (2023)

canonicalSpecs.name: Banana Daiquiri (shaken, modern)
canonicalSpecs.source: Modern craft build (aged rum + crème de banane), cf. Giffard Banane du Brésil serves

canonicalSpecs.name: Pineapple Daiquiri (on the rocks)
canonicalSpecs.source: Difford's Guide

canonicalSpecs.name: Passion Fruit Daiquiri
canonicalSpecs.source: Difford's Guide

canonicalSpecs.name: Frozen Strawberry Daiquiri (Tropical Standard)
canonicalSpecs.source: Tropical Standard (2023)

archetypes.name: Hot Buttered Rum & Coffee Grog
archetypes.definition: Aged or dark rum stirred into boiling water (or hot coffee) with a spiced butter-and-brown-sugar batter, served steaming in a warmed mug with nutmeg; the Coffee Grog version adds citrus peels and is sometimes flamed.

oleo-saccharum for syrup

archetypes.name: Zombie
archetypes.definition: A tall, deceptively smooth flash-blended punch of three contrasting rums (light/gold column, funky Jamaican, and an overproof Demerara kicker) balanced by lime and grapefruit, sweetened and spiced by falernum, cinnamon (Don's Mix) and a little grenadine, and seasoned with drops of anise and Angostura.

signature.note: At least two distinct styles: a clean column-still gold/light rum plus a Jamaican (or other pot-still) rum for funk.
151 Demerara is canonical (Lemon Hart / Hamilton). Mixed in, never floated, in the Don original; the burning 151 float is a later chain-restaurant habit.
Don: 3/4 oz lime (1934) or 1 lime + 1 lemon (c. 1950). Vic used lemon.

Use at least two. 1934 route (preferred): 1/2 oz Don's Mix (or 1/4 grapefruit + 1/4 cinnamon) + 1/2 oz falernum. c. 1950 route: 1 oz passion fruit syrup + 1 oz pineapple + lemon. Vic route: 1 oz orange curaçao + 1 oz orange juice.
6 drops (about 1/8 tsp) Pernod or Herbsaint; Smuggler's Cove uses Herbstura (Herbsaint + Angostura 1:1). Absent only from the c. 1950 printed spec.
1-2 dashes. Absent from Vic's 1946 home version.

optional.note: One teaspoon in 1934 and Smuggler's Cove: depth, not color. It must not turn the drink red (Vic's 1/2 oz is the ceiling).
Only together with passion fruit syrup.

archetypes.name: Piña Colada
archetypes.definition: Rum (vodka in the Chi Chi) with pineapple juice and sweetened cream of coconut, blended or shaken until cold, opaque and silky and garnished with pineapple and a cherry. Without both coconut and pineapple it is not a colada.

signature.note: Light Puerto Rican rum is canonical. The craft upgrade blends in a funky aged rum (Jamaican, agricole). Vodka makes it a Chi Chi and should be named that way. Up to 2 oz of rum total; a split of 2-4 rums is fine.

Fresh or 100% unsweetened juice (or fresh chunks blended in, about 1/4 cup per oz). 'Colada' means strained, as in strained pineapple. Pineapple rum or pineapple syrup can only add to the juice; neither replaces it.
Sweetened cream of coconut (Coco López, invented 1948-54) is the drink's engine: it brings the sugar, fat and coconut flavor together. Coconut rum alone is never enough coconut.

optional.note: The Caribe Hilton's published house recipe adds 1 oz of heavy cream. Use it only with little or no lime.
A squeeze brightens it (Erick Castro uses 1/2 oz). Above 1/2 oz it starts to become a coconut daiquiri.
A floated dark rum gives a brown cap that bleeds into tan streaks.
Only alongside the cream of coconut, never instead of it.
A pinch of salt, a dash of bitters or a barspoon of spice. Keep it subtle; the drink should still read as a Piña Colada.

canonicalSpecs.name: Chi Chi
canonicalSpecs.source: Mid-century Hawaiian resort drink; appears in Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide (1972). The spec is the common bar-guide version; the original amounts are not verified.

ratios.notes: sweetOz is the cream of coconut. Pineapple to coconut runs from 1:1 (Castro, shaken) to 6:1 (Caribe Hilton, blended); 3-4:1 by volume is the sweet spot for blended. Acid barely matters because the coconut fat does the balancing, so aim for 8-12 g sugar per 100 ml after dilution. Blended ABV uses a volume-aware frozen model (ice ≈ 12 oz minus liquid, clamped to 2.5-6 oz). The repo's flat ×0.9 blend dilution under-reads a Caribe Hilton colada at about 4% when it is really about 6%.

never: mint sprig as the main garnish

Blended it looks paler and frostier, with a matte, fine-grained surface domed just above the rim. Shaken it is silky, with a thin foam cap over pebble ice. aged Jamaican or rhum agricole for half the light rum
fresh pineapple chunks, blended, for the juice

a 1/2 oz black or navy rum float

part of the pineapple swapped for mango or passion fruit, but only if the name says so ('Mango Colada')
coconut water for the heavy cream in a lighter version

Unsweetened coconut milk with no added sugar, which tastes flat and greasy
More than 1/2 oz of lime: it reads as a daiquiri and can split the cream
Served up in a coupe with no ice
Watery, separated or chunky blended texture
Bitter liqueurs, anise, egg white, soda or anything fizzy
Blue curaçao that nobody asked for (that is a Blue Hawaiian)
Mint or a lime shell as garnish
Copy calling it tart, bracing, bitter or dry
Described as clear or amber: a colada is always opaque white-gold

Cream of coconut (Coco López).

Kahlúa or Tia Maria.

Coco López.

cold-brew coffee for half the coffee liqueur, to cut sweetness
coconut milk for dairy (dairy-free)
redFlags: Any citrus: it curdles the dairy and clashes with the chocolate
Pineapple, which turns it into an incoherent colada-milkshake hybrid
Copy calling it tropical-fruity or tart

archetypes.name: Coconut Daiquiri
archetypes.definition: A daiquiri sweetened with cream of coconut instead of syrup: rum, lime and Coco López shaken hard and served up, or blended. It is tart and creamy, and with no pineapple it is a daiquiri, not a colada.

signature.note: Fresh lime only.
The cream of coconut does the work of the simple syrup.

optional.note: Needed when the coconut is under 1 oz.

canonicalSpecs.name: Coconut Daiquiri (shaken, up)
canonicalSpecs.source: Representative modern spec (a daiquiri with cream of coconut as the sweetener); there is no single canonical source
canonicalSpecs.note: Shake very hard so the coconut fat emulsifies into a fine foam.

canonicalSpecs.name: Frozen Coconut Daiquiri
canonicalSpecs.source: Common published frozen spec: 2 oz white rum, 1 oz lime, 1 oz cream of coconut, 3/4 cup crushed ice

canonicalSpecs.name: Coconut Daiquiri (Montanya)
canonicalSpecs.source: Montanya Distillers house recipe

ratios.notes: Daiquiri balance, with cream of coconut as the sweetener (1 oz CoC ≈ 3/4 oz simple syrup in sugar).

never: maraschino cherry and umbrella on the up version

archetypes.look: Opaque milky white with a faint green-ivory cast from the lime and a fine, tight pale foam, served up in a coupe. Blended, it is a frosty matte white snow.
substitutions: rhum agricole blanc or cachaça for the light rum
a split with a little Jamaican rum for funk
coconut-washed rum plus simple syrup for the cream of coconut
redFlags: Adding pineapple and still calling it a daiquiri (it is now a colada)
Dairy cream with lime, which curdles
Too little lime, so it tastes like a flat colada
Coconut rum as the only coconut

archetypes.name: Miami Vice
archetypes.definition: A Piña Colada and a Strawberry Daiquiri, blended separately and poured into one tall glass as distinct red and white layers or a marbled swirl: two frozen drinks in one.

signature.note: Split between the two halves.
In the daiquiri half only.

canonicalSpecs.name: Miami Vice
canonicalSpecs.source: Composite of common published specs (1980s Florida; named for the TV show); not verified to an origin
canonicalSpecs.note: Blend each half with ice separately. Pour the daiquiri first, then the colada slowly over a spoon (layers), or pour both at once from either side (swirl).

canonicalSpecs.name: Miami Vice (even halves)
canonicalSpecs.source: Common home-bar spec reported by Chowhound and others

ratios.notes: Balance each half on its own (daiquiri half about 7.5:1, colada half about 30:1); never balance the combined drink.

archetypes.look: Two opaque frozen halves in one tall glass: coral-red strawberry daiquiri and ivory colada. Either in hard-edged layers (both frozen, so they hold their place whatever their density) or a marbled pink-and-white swirl.
substitutions: mango daiquiri for the strawberry half
aged rum in the colada half
redFlags: Blended together into one pink drink
One layer shaken liquid and the other frozen, so they mix

archetypes.name: Blue Hawaii
archetypes.definition: Harry Yee's 1957 Hilton Hawaiian Village showpiece: light rum and vodka with blue curaçao, pineapple juice and sweet-and-sour over crushed ice. It is a bright, tart pineapple sour that happens to be turquoise, with no coconut (that is the Blue Hawaiian).

signature.note: Classically 3/4 oz light rum plus 3/4 oz vodka. Keep the spirits clear so the color stays clean.
Dosed against the pineapple: 1/2 oz per 1 1/2-3 oz of juice keeps it turquoise.
Fresh lemon replaces the bottled sweet-and-sour.

canonicalSpecs.name: Blue Hawaii (Harry Yee, 1957)
canonicalSpecs.source: Harry Yee, Hilton Hawaiian Village, Waikiki, 3 January 1957, created for a Bols blue curaçao rep (Hawaii Magazine)

canonicalSpecs.name: Garret Richard's Blue Hawaii
canonicalSpecs.source: Garret Richard, Punch 'Masters of Tiki' (co-author of Tropical Standard, 2023)
canonicalSpecs.note: Flash-blend with 12 oz of crushed ice and dump into the glass.

ratios.notes: sweetOz excludes the blue curaçao (about 33 g sugar/100 ml), which also sweetens. Keep blue curaçao at roughly 1 part to 3-6 parts pineapple for turquoise.

archetypes.look: Vivid turquoise or aqua, translucent-to-hazy from the pineapple, with a white pineapple-foam head and crushed ice glittering through it. The blue-to-pineapple ratio sets the hue: too much pineapple turns it green, too little makes it electric ink-blue.
substitutions: gin for the vodka (Garret Richard)
lime for lemon
lime cordial for half the sugar and acid
redFlags: Coconut cream added, but still called a Blue Hawaii
Muddy green or teal-grey from orange juice, dark rum or grenadine

archetypes.name: Hurricane
archetypes.definition: Pat O'Brien's big New Orleans rum sour: a lot of dark or gold rum with lemon and passion fruit syrup (red Fassionola in the 1950s), served in the hurricane-lamp glass over crushed ice. Passion fruit is non-negotiable.

signature.note: Classically 4 oz. This is a big, strong drink, and dark rum is the default.
Syrup is canonical. Unsweetened purée needs added syrup.
Lemon in Pat O'Brien's lineage.

canonicalSpecs.name: Hurricane (Pat O'Brien's, 1956)
canonicalSpecs.source: Louis Culligan, head bartender at Pat O'Brien's, New Orleans, in Cabaret magazine (1956); the bar's 1940s origin is undocumented in detail

canonicalSpecs.name: Hurricane (Beachbum Berry)
canonicalSpecs.source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010)

canonicalSpecs.name: Hurricane (Smuggler's Cove)
canonicalSpecs.source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)
garnish: cocktail umbrella in a lemon wedge

canonicalSpecs.name: Hurricane (fresh modern)
canonicalSpecs.source: Liquor.com fresh-ingredient version

ratios.notes: The classic is 2 rum : 1 lemon : 1 passion fruit syrup. A single-serve generated version can scale to 2-3 oz rum, keeping 2:1:1.

archetypes.look: Cloudy and glowing. The Fassionola or grenadine versions are hurricane-lamp red-orange. Fresh passion fruit with dark rum gives golden apricot to amber-orange, sometimes with dark seed specks from purée. Tall in the curvy glass over crushed ice, under an orange-and-cherry flag.
substitutions: black blended rum for dark Jamaican
lime for half the lemon
1/4 oz grenadine for the Fassionola red
a little overproof floated on top
redFlags: Weak 1 oz rum pour: a Hurricane is strong
Copy calling it gentle or delicate

archetypes.name: Resort Rum Punch (Rum Runner, Bahama Mama)
archetypes.definition: The beach-bar fruit punch: one or two rums with a pair of fruit or flavor liqueurs (blackberry and banana, coffee and coconut, apricot, Galliano), pineapple or orange juice, a real squeeze of citrus and grenadine. It is only good when fresh citrus keeps the liqueur sugar in check.

signature.note: Often a light-and-dark or base-and-overproof pair.
Total liqueur up to 2 oz, at most 2 kinds. This is the drink's signature.
Fresh citrus is what separates a good one from a cloying one.

optional.note: Rum Runner and red Bahama Mama.
Lost Lake uses a little coconut syrup. More than 1/2 oz turns it into a colada.

canonicalSpecs.name: Rum Runner (Holiday Isle)
canonicalSpecs.source: Tiki John Ebert, Holiday Isle Tiki Bar, Islamorada, Florida Keys, 1972; spec per Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), cross-checked with ultimatemaitai.com

canonicalSpecs.name: Rum Runner (modern, shaken)
canonicalSpecs.source: Difford's Guide 'Rum Runner' (from search summary)

canonicalSpecs.name: Bahama Mama (coffee style)
canonicalSpecs.source: Gary Regan, The Bartender's Bible (1991); follows the coffee-liqueur version credited to Oswald Greenslade, Nassau Beach Hotel, 1961

canonicalSpecs.name: Bahama Mama (Lost Lake)
canonicalSpecs.source: Paul McGee, Lost Lake, Chicago; Punch 'Rescuing the Bahama Mama'

lines.orig: a scant amount of Giffard Banane du Brésil (amount not confirmed)

canonicalSpecs.name: Goombay Smash
canonicalSpecs.source: Miss Emily's Blue Bee Bar, Green Turtle Cay, Bahamas (secret recipe); the common copycat spec

ratios.notes: The liqueurs (0.5-2 oz total) are the main sweetener and carry real alcohol. Fresh citrus at 1/2 oz or more is the difference between a good one and syrup.

archetypes.look: Rum Runner, shaken: deep ruby-garnet with a purple cast from the blackberry, shading orange where the pineapple shows; frozen it is an opaque magenta-pink slush. Red Bahama Mama: a red-orange sunset, often with the grenadine sunk to the bottom for a gradient. Coffee Bahama Mama: hazy amber-brown. Goombay Smash: hazy golden yellow.
substitutions: crème de mûre for blackberry brandy
aged Jamaican for dark rum
pomegranate molasses-sharpened grenadine for commercial
Jamaican overproof white for 151
redFlags: Commercial red-dye grenadine and coconut rum as the whole drink

archetypes.name: Hawaiian Mai Tai
archetypes.definition: The Waikiki hotel Mai Tai: light rum, orange curaçao and orgeat lengthened with pineapple and orange juice, finished with a dark-rum float. It is a resort punch that legitimately carries the Mai Tai name in Hawaii, but it must never be called Trader Vic's 1944 original.

signature.note: This, with the curaçao, is the Mai Tai DNA.
Floated last; the visual signature.

optional.note: A good version always has some lime.
Some hotel versions, for a sunset tint.

canonicalSpecs.name: Royal Hawaiian Mai Tai (current)
canonicalSpecs.source: Royal Hawaiian Hotel, Waikiki; current house recipe with Old Lahaina rums (Wikipedia / ultimatemaitai.com). The 1953 Matson-menu original had no juice; see the mai-tai archetype for the 1956 recipe.

canonicalSpecs.name: Hawaiian Mai Tai (hotel-bar composite)
canonicalSpecs.source: Composite of Hawaiian hotel-bar specs; recalled, not verified

ratios.notes: baseOz includes the float. The current Royal Hawaiian recipe has no lime (ratio 29); a generated version should add 1/2 oz lime to land at 13-16.

archetypes.look: A cloudy sunset orange-gold body (pineapple and orange) over crushed ice, under a dark mahogany rum float. The float sits as a brown cap and bleeds downward into an amber band, the classic Hawaiian gradient. Pineapple flag, cherry and orchid.
substitutions: aged Jamaican rum for the dark float
lime added for balance
orgeat raised to 1/2 oz
redFlags: Labelled 'the original Mai Tai' or credited to Trader Vic
No orgeat or curaçao (then it is just rum punch)

archetypes.name: Tropical Itch
archetypes.definition: Harry Yee's late-1950s Hilton Hawaiian Village tall passion fruit punch of bourbon and dark rum with orange curaçao and bitters. An overproof float goes on top and a bamboo back-scratcher stands in the glass.

signature.note: The unusual bourbon-plus-rum base is the identity.
Sweetened Hawaiian passion fruit juice in the original; purée plus syrup in craft versions.

optional.note: Curaçao in the original; allspice or falernum in craft versions.

canonicalSpecs.name: Tropical Itch (Harry Yee)
canonicalSpecs.source: Harry Yee, Hawaiian Village Hotel, Waikiki, late 1950s; reconstruction as published by Kaiser Penguin and others (the original calls for 4-8 oz passion fruit juice and a 3/4-1 1/4 oz overproof float). Amounts are approximate.
canonicalSpecs.note: Fill the glass with crushed ice, stir in everything but the overproof, then float it.

canonicalSpecs.name: Tropical Itch (Three Dots and a Dash)
canonicalSpecs.source: Three Dots and a Dash, Chicago (Imbibe / Whisky Advocate)

canonicalSpecs.name: Tropical Itch (Tern Club)
canonicalSpecs.source: Jocelyn Morin & Ryan Shanley, Tern Club, Knoxville; Punch 'Tropical Itch'

ratios.notes: baseOz excludes the overproof float, which adds 1/2-1 oz on top.

never: cocktail umbrella instead of the back-scratcher

archetypes.look: Tall, cloudy yellow-orange passion fruit body over crushed ice, under a thin amber-brown overproof float. A bamboo back-scratcher sticks out of the glass like a stir stick.
substitutions: rye for bourbon
allspice dram for curaçao
purée plus syrup for sweetened juice

archetypes.name: Pineapple-Shell Punch (Pi Yi, Lapu Lapu)
archetypes.definition: A two-rum passion fruit and citrus punch blended with ice and served inside a hollowed-out pineapple, with the crown as a lid. The fruit is the cup, so pineapple is in the drink as well as around it.

signature.note: A light-and-dark or Puerto Rican and Martinique pair.
Lime in the Pi Yi; orange, lemon and lime in the Lapu Lapu.
Pi Yi yes; Chief Lapu Lapu takes its pineapple from the shell itself.

canonicalSpecs.name: Pi Yi (Beachbum Berry)
canonicalSpecs.source: Don the Beachcomber's Pi Yi as given in Jeff Berry, Intoxica! (2002)
garnish: the pineapple crown as a lid
canonicalSpecs.note: Blend with 8 oz of ice for about a minute, pour into the hollowed pineapple and top up with crushed ice.

canonicalSpecs.name: Pi Yi (Don the Beachcomber, Hawaii)
canonicalSpecs.source: Don the Beachcomber's Hawaiian-era recipe (Hawaii Tropical Rum Drinks & Cuisine by Don the Beachcomber), via Tiki Central. The Negrita rum amount is not shown in the source summary; 1 oz is an assumption.
canonicalSpecs.note: Blend with cracked ice for 30 seconds and pour into a hollowed pineapple with the top replaced.

canonicalSpecs.name: Chief Lapu Lapu
canonicalSpecs.source: Mid-century standard recipe per Jeff Berry (Grog Log 1998; Remixed 2010 swaps the sour mix for lemon and simple syrup). Origin unknown; it was the Royal Hawaiian Hotel's (Laguna Beach) signature drink. Exact amounts not verified.

ratios.notes: A 20 oz pineapple shell is mostly filled with crushed ice; pour 6-8 oz of liquid.

required: hollowed pineapple with crown lid (or a big snifter)

archetypes.look: Hidden inside the fruit. When glimpsed, a pale golden, frothy (blended) or cloudy apricot-orange (shaken, with orange juice) liquid packed with crushed ice under the pineapple crown, with a straw poking through.
substitutions: a large snifter for the pineapple
apricot for peach
aged agricole for gold rum
redFlags: Served in a pineapple but with no pineapple or passion fruit in the drink
Too small a pour for a 20 oz shell (top up with crushed ice instead)

archetypes.name: Sunrise & Float (Layered Presentation)
archetypes.definition: A built or gently shaken long drink designed to show its density: a heavy, colored syrup or liqueur (grenadine, cassis, blackberry) sinks to the bottom and blooms upward into a sunrise gradient, and/or a light, colored spirit (dark or overproof rum, sherry) floats as a dark cap. It is never stirred before it reaches the guest.

signature.note: An opaque juice body (SG about 1.03-1.05) lets the sink stay put. A clear soda body shows a cleaner gradient but mixes faster.
Needs SG of at least 1.15: grenadine about 1.21, cassis about 1.15. Dark and colored, or the effect is invisible.

optional.note: SG of 0.95 or less; pour over the back of a barspoon onto the ice cap.
Recommended: a squeeze of lime rescues the Trident version from flatness.

canonicalSpecs.name: Tequila Sunrise
canonicalSpecs.source: Bobby Lozoff & Billy Rice, The Trident, Sausalito, early 1970s; popularized by the Rolling Stones' 1972 tour
canonicalSpecs.note: Build tequila and orange juice over ice, then pour the grenadine down the inside of the glass so it sinks. Do not stir.

canonicalSpecs.name: Tequila Sunrise (Arizona Biltmore)
canonicalSpecs.source: Gene Sulit, Arizona Biltmore, Phoenix, 1930s-40s
canonicalSpecs.note: The cassis sinks into a purple-red base under clear, fizzy lime soda.

canonicalSpecs.name: Hawaiian Mai Tai float (reference)
canonicalSpecs.source: Royal Hawaiian Hotel current recipe; see the hawaiian-mai-tai archetype

ratios.notes: Layer physics: SG ≈ 1 + 0.0038 × sugar(g/100 ml) − 0.0013 × ABV. Grenadine ≈ 1.21, cassis ≈ 1.15, orange juice ≈ 1.04, a shaken punch ≈ 1.01-1.03, 40% dark rum ≈ 0.95, 75% overproof ≈ 0.90. A sink holds if it is 0.12 or more above the body; a float holds if it is 0.05 or more below.

archetypes.look: A vertical gradient. Deep crimson at the base, from the grenadine pool, blends through coral and orange into yellow-gold juice at the top; cassis gives a purple-black base under clear soda. With a float, a mahogany cap sits on the ice and feathers down. Juice bodies are opaque, so the bands show at the glass wall.
substitutions: rum for tequila (Rum Sunrise)
pineapple or passion fruit for orange juice
hibiscus syrup for grenadine (deeper magenta)
a dark-rum float on any juice-forward punch
redFlags: A "sunrise" that has been stirred or shaken after the sink went in, so the gradient is gone
A clear sink (simple syrup) that cannot be seen
A float with a clear spirit (invisible) or on a dense, sweet body where a 40% rum is described as "floating" on a dry 15% sour
Sinks and floats in a blended drink

archetypes.name: Scorpion Bowl (Communal Orgeat Bowls)
archetypes.definition: Trader Vic's communal punch for three or more, served in a ceramic bowl with long straws: light rum and brandy (sometimes gin or white wine) with lemon, orange juice and orgeat. It is lighter per sip than it looks, and often has a flaming overproof crater and a gardenia.

signature.note: Bowl totals are 3-6 times this.
Brandy is the signature second spirit.

optional.note: Poured into the central cone and lit. It is not mixed in and should be extinguished before drinking.

canonicalSpecs.name: Scorpion Punch (1946, for twelve)
canonicalSpecs.source: Trader Vic's Book of Food & Drink (1946): 1 1/2 bottles Puerto Rican rum, 2 oz gin, 2 oz brandy, 1 pt lemon, 1/2 pt orange juice, 1/2 pt orgeat, 1/2 bottle white wine, 2 sprigs mint. Rest 2 hours, add ice. Bottle = fifth (25.6 oz).
canonicalSpecs.note: Let stand 2 hours; add ice and serve.

canonicalSpecs.name: Scorpion (for three or four)
canonicalSpecs.source: Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide, revised (1972)
canonicalSpecs.note: Blend with 2 scoops of shaved ice, pour into the bowl and fill with ice cubes.

canonicalSpecs.name: Kava Bowl
canonicalSpecs.source: Trader Vic, c. 1942 (Difford's Guide, after Vic's Bartender's Guide)
canonicalSpecs.note: Blend with 3 scoops of shaved ice.

canonicalSpecs.name: Flaming Volcano (Chinese-American restaurant style)
canonicalSpecs.source: Common recipe given by Wikipedia (Flaming volcano); the restaurant versions vary widely
canonicalSpecs.note: Blend everything except the 151 with 4 scoops of crushed ice. Pour the 151 into the crater and light it.

canonicalSpecs.name: Scorpion Bowl (Jacoby's)
canonicalSpecs.source: Jacoby's Tiki Bar (Australian Bartender)

ratios.notes: Per serving. Bowl total = per serving × servings (2-6); a 64 oz Scorpion bowl takes about 18-24 oz of liquid plus ice. Vic's bowls are tart (about 5.6). The 1946 twelve-person punch is an outlier at about 16.6% ABV.

archetypes.look: A wide ceramic bowl of pale, cloudy orange-yellow (orange juice, lemon and milky orgeat) packed with ice, with a gardenia floating and several long straws. A blue flame dances in the central volcano crater. The Kava Bowl is pink from the grenadine.
substitutions: gin for some of the brandy
white wine to lengthen a batch
shaved ice in a bowl instead of a blender for a crowd
redFlags: Built for one in a bowl
The 151 crater fuel mixed into the drink
Copy that encourages drinking it fast

archetypes.name: Volcano Bowl (Beachcomber Grog Bowl)
archetypes.definition: A Don the Beachcomber-style bowl for two to four: a three-rum grog of grapefruit, lime and a dark sweetener (maple, honey or demerara) shaken over crushed ice. A flaming lime shell (or the bowl's crater) burns in the middle.

signature.note: Demerara-led, about 3:2:1 Demerara : gold Jamaican : gold Puerto Rican.
White grapefruit.
Maple in the Berry spec.

canonicalSpecs.name: Volcano Bowl
canonicalSpecs.source: Don the Beachcomber mid-century California bowl, as given by Jeff 'Beachbum' Berry (via cocktail sites; the exact book is unconfirmed)
garnish: flaming lime shell: spent shell floated upside down with a bread crouton soaked in lemon extract, lit
canonicalSpecs.note: Shake with a heaping scoop of crushed ice; pour unstrained into the bowl and top with crushed ice.

ratios.notes: Per serving (3 servings in the canonical bowl). Tart grog balance: grapefruit is both sour and weak.

archetypes.look: Translucent-to-cloudy amber-gold (grapefruit and Demerara) over crushed ice in a dark lava-glazed bowl. A small flame flickers in the center from a floating lime shell or the crater.
substitutions: honey for maple
black blended rum for part of the Demerara
redFlags: Sweet orange punch passed off as a Volcano Bowl

archetypes.name: Zero-Proof Tiki
archetypes.definition: A non-alcoholic drink built on a real tiki skeleton (sour, sweet, spice, weak) that replaces what rum gives (body, bite, bitterness and dryness) with tea tannin, ginger or chile heat, a spice syrup, a pinch of salt and a textural element like coconut or orgeat. It should not be a juice cup; it should taste like tiki.

signature.note: Fresh citrus is the backbone.
This is where the tiki identity lives. Use 1-2 syrups and make at least one of them spiced or nutty.
Tea for tannin and dryness, ginger for burn, coconut for body, cold brew for bitterness. Saline sharpens everything.
One or two fruits, no more. Keep juice well under half the drink, or it reads as a fruit cup.

canonicalSpecs.name: Virgin Piña Colada (Nada Colada)
canonicalSpecs.source: Common bar spec; the lime "backbone" tip is standard modern practice
canonicalSpecs.note: Frozen pineapple chunks in place of some of the ice keep it thick.

canonicalSpecs.name: Zero-Proof Navy Grog (template)
canonicalSpecs.source: Illustrative template, not a historical spec: Navy Grog structure with chilled strong black tea in place of the rum (the approach of Three Dots and a Dash's house-made 'spirits' and Derek Brown's Mindful Mixology)

lines.orig: strong black tea, chilled (Lapsang souchong for smoke)

canonicalSpecs.name: Zero-Proof Mai Tai (template)
canonicalSpecs.source: Illustrative template following published NA Mai Tai practice: toasted orgeat carries the body, tea and a little demerara stand in for the rum

lines.orig: fresh orange juice, standing in for the curaçao

canonicalSpecs.name: Ginger Pineapple Swizzle (zero-proof template)
canonicalSpecs.source: Illustrative template: Queen's Park Swizzle structure with ginger syrup for burn

ratios.notes: With no ethanol, Arnold's curve gives only about 23% shaken dilution. Target 8-11 g sugar and 0.8-1.0 g acid per 100 ml (colada-style: 10-12 sugar, 0.5 acid). Replace the spirit volume with tea, coconut water or soda rather than more juice.

required: full tiki garnish (it must look like a tiki drink)
never: a different, lesser garnish than the boozy drinks get

archetypes.look: Indistinguishable from its boozy sibling: the same vessel, the same ice and the same garnish. Tea-based drinks are translucent amber; coconut-based ones opaque ivory; passion and guava ones cloudy orange-pink.
substitutions: commercial NA rum alternative for the tea (mapped to nothing in the pantry yet)
Lapsang souchong for smoky Demerara character
cold brew for bitterness (coffee grog style)
falernum syrup for velvet falernum
glycerin-based NA bitters for Angostura
redFlags: Juice in a glass with an umbrella
Angostura dashes or extracts in a drink sold as zero-proof (Angostura is 44.7% ABV)
Velvet falernum, allspice dram or any liqueur
Over-diluted: no ethanol means it needs less water, so shake shorter
Cloying because the acid was cut
A downgraded garnish or plain glass for the NA guest
